passage: "So people think I'm restless. And fine, I am, a bit. My name's Vidya, I'm sixteen, and there's always a pen cap in my mouth. I tap my foot through every class. To study I need loud music, really loud, or my brain won't sit still. My best friend Nilesh is the opposite. At the school fest he wore ear defenders and ate only the plain parathas he brought from home. Some people laughed. But he knows himself. That's what we worked out together. We both have bodies that react strongly, just in different directions. So I carry a chewy bracelet instead of wrecking pens, and I ask to sit at the back so my tapping doesn't bother anyone. Nilesh plans his quiet corner before every event. It's not weird. It's a plan."

qa.q: What did Nilesh bring from home to the school fest?
qa.a: Plain parathas, and he wore ear defenders.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to feel about being called restless?
qa.a: Vidya accepts it without shame and seems proud that Vidya and Nilesh understand themselves well enough to plan.

qa.q: What choices does Vidya make to manage the need for movement?
qa.a: Vidya carries a chewy bracelet instead of chewing pens and sits at the back so the tapping doesn't bother anyone.

qa.q: How might the people who laughed at Nilesh see him if they heard Vidya?
qa.a: They might see him as someone who knows what his body needs and plans for it, not as someone strange.

grounding: It shows a teenager who chews, fidgets and craves loud music and a friend who covers his ears and avoids foods, both using self-knowledge to plan.

passage: My brother Omkar is fifteen, and at our cousin's wedding I watched him closely. I can't say what was in his head, only what I saw. When the band started, he pressed both hands over his ears and stepped behind a pillar. At dinner he took only curd rice and left the fried items untouched. But he wasn't sulking. Before we went, he had asked Mummy which hall had the quiet garden, and he'd packed earplugs in his pocket. When the dancing began, he nodded to me and went out to that garden. Later he came back in for the photos, smiling properly. "I just needed ten minutes," he told me. "I know how much noise I can take." I'm Neelam, by the way. I used to call him boring. I don't now.

What does Omkar's line 'I know how much noise I can take' suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he understands his own needs and feels confident planning around them.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's choices helped him enjoy the wedding?
qa.a: He asked about the quiet garden in advance, carried earplugs and took a short break before the photos.

qa.q: How has Neelam's view of Omkar changed?
qa.a: Neelam used to call him boring, but now sees that he is managing the noise wisely.

grounding: A sibling watches a teenager who covers his ears in a crowd and avoids certain foods, and sees how his self-knowledge lets him plan.
